questions.enonce_markdown:
Compound A of molecular mass $103\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ contains carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen. On analysis it is found to contain 46.6 % carbon, 8.74 % hydrogen, 13.6 % nitrogen and 31.1 % oxygen.

Calculate:

(i) The empirical formula of A:

(ii) The molecular formula of A

(iii) How can you identify the presence of nitrogen in compound A? Give the reagents and expected results only.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Empirical formula.** Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass, then by the smallest result:

| Element | % by mass | % / RAM = moles in 100 g | Ratio (divide by 0.971) | Whole numbers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | 46.6 | $46.6/12 = 3.88$ | 4.00 | 4 |
| H | 8.74 | $8.74/1 = 8.74$ | 9.00 | 9 |
| N | 13.6 | $13.6/14 = 0.971$ | 1.00 | 1 |
| O | 31.1 | $31.1/16 = 1.94$ | 2.00 | 2 |

**Empirical formula: $\mathrm{C_4H_9NO_2}$.**

**(ii) Molecular formula.** Mass of the empirical formula: $4(12) + 9(1) + 14 + 2(16) = 103$. Since the molecular mass is $103$, $n = 103/103 = 1$.

**Molecular formula: $\mathrm{C_4H_9NO_2}$.**

**(iii) Test for nitrogen (Lassaigne sodium fusion test).** Fuse a small sample with a piece of **sodium metal** in an ignition tube, heat until red hot and plunge the tube into distilled water; boil and filter. The filtrate contains sodium cyanide, $\mathrm{NaCN}$, formed from the carbon and nitrogen of the compound. Add freshly prepared **iron(II) sulphate solution**, boil, then add a few drops of **iron(III) chloride** and acidify with dilute sulphuric acid (or hydrochloric acid). **Result: a Prussian blue colour or precipitate ($\mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}$) shows that nitrogen is present.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The organic compound P, named 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, exhibits isomerism,

(i) Draw two isomeric structures of P.

(ii) State the type of isomerism exhibited by the two structural forms of P.

(iii) Give a test you would use to distinguish the isomers of P in b(i) above.

(iv) The compound P can be obtained from the reaction of ethanal and HCN. Write a mechanism for the reaction.

(v) What name is given to the type of reaction between ethanal and HCN? *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** P is $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}$. Carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups ($-\mathrm{H}$, $-\mathrm{CH_3}$, $-\mathrm{OH}$, $-\mathrm{CN}$): it is a **chiral (asymmetric) carbon**, so P exists as two non-superimposable mirror-image structures:

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

**(ii)** **Optical isomerism** (enantiomerism): the two isomers are enantiomers, the (R) and the (S) forms.

**(iii)** Use **plane-polarised light in a polarimeter**: the two enantiomers **rotate the plane of polarisation by equal angles in opposite directions** (one dextrorotatory, +, the other laevorotatory, -). Apart from this, they have identical physical and chemical properties.

**(iv) Mechanism: nucleophilic addition** of hydrogen cyanide to ethanal. The reaction needs the cyanide ion, produced from the weak acid HCN with a trace of base (e.g. $\mathrm{HCN} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CN^-} + \mathrm{H_2O}$, or KCN added).

Step 1 (slow): the cyanide ion, a nucleophile, uses its lone pair to attack the **electron-poor carbon** of the polar carbonyl group ($\overset{\delta+}{\mathrm{C}}=\overset{\delta-}{\mathrm{O}}$). The C=O $\pi$ bond breaks heterolytically and its pair of electrons goes onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide intermediate:

$\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + {:}\mathrm{CN^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(O^-)CN}$

(curly arrows: one from the lone pair on the C of $\mathrm{CN^-}$ to the carbonyl carbon; one from the C=O bond to the oxygen.)

Step 2 (fast): the negatively charged oxygen takes a proton from a molecule of HCN (or of water), giving the product and regenerating the cyanide ion:

$\mathrm{CH_3CH(O^-)CN} + \mathrm{HCN} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN} + \mathrm{CN^-}$

Overall: $\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCN} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}$. Because the carbonyl group is planar, $\mathrm{CN^-}$ attacks equally from either face, so equal amounts of the (R) and (S) forms are made: a **racemic mixture**, which has **no effect on plane-polarised light**.

**(v)** The reaction is a **nucleophilic addition** (an addition reaction of a carbonyl compound, by a nucleophile).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Give the reagents and observations to distinguish the following pairs of compounds:

(i) $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3C{=}CH}$ *(as printed)*

(ii) $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$

(iii) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$ *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The second formula is printed with a double bond and is incomplete; it is read as **propyne, $\mathrm{CH_3C{\equiv}CH}$**, so the pair is propene and propyne. Bromine water or acidified $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ is decolourised by both, so it does not distinguish them. Use **ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollens' reagent without the aldehyde)**:

- **propyne** (a terminal alkyne, with an acidic $\equiv\mathrm{C{-}H}$) gives a **white precipitate** of silver propynide: $\mathrm{CH_3C{\equiv}CH} + [\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3C{\equiv}CAg}\downarrow + \mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{NH_4^+}$;
- **propene**: no reaction, no precipitate.

(Ammoniacal copper(I) chloride gives a red precipitate with propyne and nothing with propene.)

**(ii)** Use **Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal silver nitrate, warmed gently): **ethanal** is oxidised and gives a **silver mirror** (grey-black precipitate of silver); **propanone** gives **no reaction**. (Alternative: Fehling's or Benedict's solution, warmed: ethanal gives a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, propanone gives no change.)

**(iii)** Shake each compound with water and test the solution with **damp red litmus paper (or universal indicator)**: **ethylamine** is a base, so the solution **turns red litmus blue** (pH about 11-12); **ethanamide is neutral** and the litmus is unchanged. A confirming test: add **copper(II) sulphate solution**: ethylamine gives a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess to a **deep blue solution** (complex), ethanamide gives no change.
